title: What's missing
hookLine: look for gaps: body, heart, mind, others, the sacred; the young Siddhartha's palace hid what was missing
tomorrow: two tiny coins, and Jesus says she gave more than all of them. how?

lines: A PALACE WITH NOTHING HARD IN VIEW.
A BODY CARRIED TO THE FIRE.
cards: Four sights got past the wall. The Buddhist story says the young prince Siddhartha grew up in a palace where his father kept every hard thing out of view. No one old, no one sick, nothing dying in the gardens.
But on rides out with his charioteer, Channa, the prince saw an old man, bent and shaking. Then a man burning with sickness. Then a body being carried to the fire.
Each time he asked, does this happen to everyone? Each time Channa said yes. And then, a fourth sight.

teach.b: A wandering renunciant, head shaved, in a simple robe, calm in a way the prince had never seen. Here was someone who had looked straight at old age, sickness and death and gone looking for a way through.
The story says Siddhartha left the palace soon after to look for it himself. Here's the teaching. In the Buddhist telling, the road begins with honest seeing.
The Buddha's first noble truth names dukkha: suffering, the unsatisfactoriness that comes with being alive. The palace wasn't evil. It was comfortable.

What it was missing was the truth past the wall, and a path. Buddhist tellings put the four sights at the start of the whole road, and some Buddhists reflect on aging, sickness and death on purpose. Not to be gloomy.
To stop the palace from lying. Now turn it to your own practice.
Notice that the father's mistake was building something that felt complete.
A practice can do the same: plenty of reading, say, and nothing for the body. Lots of quiet, and nobody else in it. So walk the walls slowly.
Mind. Other people. The sacred, however you name it.
You're not looking for everything that's wrong. You're looking for one gap, honestly seen, the way the prince finally saw.

how: Buddhists retell the four sights as the start of the Buddha's search, and some recite the Five Remembrances, reflecting that aging, sickness and death come to everyone, as a regular practice.

o: the one gap your practice leaves out, honestly seen
every mistake you've ever made in your practice
something you lost and need to buy again

games.q: the four sights: tap the pairs.
p: every hard thing kept out of view
the charioteer: yes, it comes to all
the suffering the first truth names

s: the palace in the story was a cruel place
it was comfortable. what it lacked was the truth past the wall, and a path.
the fourth sight showed the prince someone looking for a way through
a calm wanderer who had faced aging, sickness and death and set out on a path.
a good practice should feel complete, with nothing missing
feeling complete was the palace's problem. honest seeing starts with finding a gap.

games.q: a friend's routine is all podcasts and journaling, and he hasn't seen another person outside work in weeks. he says it's going great. what fits the four sights?
o: look honestly past the wall: his routine may be missing other people.
if it feels complete to him, there's nothing worth looking at.
he should drop the whole routine, since it's obviously failing.
games.why: the palace felt complete and still hid what mattered. honest seeing finds one gap, without condemning the rest.

practice: Move your hands slowly through five places: a hand on your belly for the body, on your chest for the heart, on your forehead for the mind, one hand open in front of you for other people, both palms up for the sacred.
Stay a few breaths at each. Notice where the hand feels like it has least to hold.

wordCard.voice: What's missing: the gap in your practice, among body, heart, mind, others and the sacred, the way the four sights showed the prince what the palace hid.

orig.note: Pali: suffering, unsatisfactoriness; named in the Buddha's first noble truth.

carryVoice: Keep this: one gap. The palace felt complete, and that was the problem. Day 1593, done.
